title: La-5 / La-5F / La-5FN (IL-2)

sources.title: JoyPro cockpit catalog (from the IL-2 and real aircraft manuals)

intro: The Lavochkin La-5 is a Soviet single-seat fighter of the Second World War with a big radial engine in the nose. The cockpit is small and plain. The left hand works the engine levers and the trim wheels, the right hand the stick with the firing button, the bomb button and the brake lever.

areas.name: Gunsight
areas.text: The aiming sight sits on top of the instrument panel, right in front of the pilot's eyes.

panels.name: PBP-1b reflector gunsight
panels.text: The PBP-1b reflector gunsight is the sight with which the pilot aims. It projects a glowing aiming mark onto a glass in front of the pilot's eyes. A simple ring-and-bead sight is the backup.
panels.context: The pilot looks through the sight in every attack with guns, rockets or bombs.

controls.name: Reflector glass (gun sight)
controls.text: This is a clear glass plate in front of the pilot. A lit aiming mark, the reticle, is projected onto it, so the pilot sees the mark floating over the outside world. The pilot puts the mark on the target before firing.
controls.context: The sight serves the guns, the rockets and the bombs alike. The lamp behind the glass needs electricity.

controls.name: Sight lamp and brightness control
controls.text: This control belongs to the lamp that lights the aiming mark. Turning it changes how bright the mark is.
controls.context: The pilot makes the mark bright enough to see against the sky or the ground, but not so bright that it dazzles.

controls.name: Back-up ring and bead sight
controls.text: This is a simple mechanical sight made of a ring and a small bead. Looking through the ring at the bead shows where the guns point. It needs no electricity and no lamp.
controls.context: The pilot can use it when the lit sight fails or is damaged. It is the plain emergency way of aiming.

areas.name: Instrument panel
areas.text: The board in front of the pilot with the dials for speed, height, direction, engine and electrics.

panels.name: Instrument panel
panels.text: The instrument panel is the board in front of the pilot. It carries the dials that show speed, height and direction, the dials for the engine, and the lights for the wheels.
panels.context: The pilot scans it all the time in flight. The engine dials say when the engine runs too hot or loses oil pressure.

controls.name: Clock with stopwatch
controls.text: This is the flight clock. It shows the time of day and has a stopwatch hand to time short things, for example how long a leg of the flight takes.
controls.context: Planes of this time had no navigation screens. A pilot judged how far he had flown from speed and time, so the clock was important.

controls.name: Airspeed indicator (km/h)
controls.text: This dial shows how fast the plane moves through the air, in kilometres per hour. The faster the plane flies, the further the needle turns.
controls.context: The pilot watches it at take-off, in the climb and when landing. Too slow and the wings stop carrying the plane, too fast can damage it.

controls.name: Tachometer (engine RPM)
controls.text: This dial shows how fast the engine turns, in rotations per minute (RPM). A higher number means the engine and propeller spin faster.
controls.context: The propeller pitch lever sets this number. The pilot reads the dial to check that the engine runs at the speed chosen for take-off, climb or cruise.

controls.name: Fuel contents gauge
controls.text: This dial shows how much fuel is left in the tanks. It is like the fuel gauge of a car.
controls.context: The pilot checks it to know how long the plane can keep flying. Fighters of this time carried little fuel, so the gauge is watched often.

controls.name: Altimeter (height gauge)
controls.text: This dial shows how high the plane is. It measures the height from the air pressure, which gets lower the higher the plane climbs.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to hold a height, to know when the thin air needs a different engine setting, and to keep clear of the ground on the way down.

controls.name: Magnetic compass
controls.text: This is a compass. It shows the direction the plane's nose points, using the Earth's magnetic field, as a hiking compass does.
controls.context: With the clock and a map it is how a pilot of this time finds the way. The pilot reads it to fly a chosen direction.

controls.name: Boost gauge (manifold pressure)
controls.text: This dial shows how hard air is pushed into the engine. This push is called boost. More boost means more engine power. The throttle lever sets it.
controls.context: The pilot watches the boost during take-off and combat, so the engine gets the power it needs without being pushed too far.

controls.name: Engine triple gauge (oil and fuel)
controls.text: Three small dials sit in one case. They show the oil temperature, the oil pressure and the fuel pressure of the engine.
controls.context: These numbers tell the pilot if the engine is healthy. A fall in oil or fuel pressure, or oil that gets too hot, is a warning.

controls.name: Voltmeter (electric voltage)
controls.text: This dial shows the voltage of the plane's electricity, which says how well the electrical system is working. It is like the battery meter of a car.
controls.context: The pilot looks at it to see that the generator is running and feeding the lights, the sight and the radio.

controls.name: RSI-4 radio receiver
controls.text: This is the receiver of the plane's radio set, called RSI-4. It receives the voices of other pilots and of the ground. It has a tuning scale on the panel.
controls.context: The radio lets pilots in a formation hear orders. The transmit button is on the throttle, and the tuning and volume knobs are on the right side.

controls.name: Course indicator (PDI)
controls.text: This instrument has a needle that shows whether the plane is left or right of the course it should follow. The pilot turns the plane until the needle sits in the centre.
controls.context: It helps the pilot to fly a chosen direction without watching the compass all the time. It belongs to the flight instruments.

controls.name: Turn and slip indicator
controls.text: This instrument has a needle that shows how fast the plane is turning and a ball in a curved tube. The ball shows whether the plane slides sideways in the turn.
controls.context: The pilot keeps the ball in the middle with the rudder. A centred ball means a clean, efficient turn. The instrument also helps when flying in cloud.

controls.name: Variometer (climb and sink rate)
controls.text: This dial shows how fast the plane is climbing or sinking. The needle moves up for a climb and down for a descent.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to hold a steady climb or descent, for example when approaching to land.

controls.name: Oil temperature gauge
controls.text: This dial shows how hot the engine oil is. The oil lubricates the engine and also carries away heat. The pilot can change the opening of the oil radiator to keep it in range.
controls.context: Oil that is too hot warns of trouble. The pilot opens the oil radiator shutters to cool it and closes them when the oil is too cold.

controls.name: Ammeter (generator current)
controls.text: This dial shows the electric current flowing to or from the battery. It tells whether the generator is charging the battery or the battery is giving power away.
controls.context: The pilot reads it together with the voltmeter. If the battery gives power all the time, the generator may not be working.

controls.name: Oxygen apparatus (breathing gauge)
controls.text: This is the gauge of the breathing system. It shows the pressure of the oxygen supply and how much oxygen flows. At high altitude the air is too thin to breathe well, so the pilot takes extra oxygen.
controls.context: The pilot needs it on high flights. Close to the ground it is not used.

controls.name: Brake pressure gauge
controls.text: This dial shows the air pressure that works the wheel brakes. The brakes of these planes work with compressed air, so the dial tells how much braking power is there.
controls.context: The pilot checks it before landing. The brake lever on the stick lets this air into the brakes.

controls.name: Magneto switch (ignition)

positions.text: Ignition is off; the engine gets no sparks and stops.

positions.name: Left
positions.text: Only the left magneto makes sparks. The pilot can use this to test it.

positions.name: Right
positions.text: Only the right magneto makes sparks. The pilot can use this to test it.

positions.name: Both (1+2)
positions.text: Both magnetos make sparks. This is the normal position for flying.

controls.text: This switch controls the ignition, the sparks that light the fuel in the engine. The engine has two magnetos, which are small generators for the sparks, so it still runs if one fails. The switch turns them on and off.
controls.context: The pilot sets it to both magnetos for flight and to 0 to stop the sparks. In a test the pilot may use each magneto alone.

controls.name: Landing gear lights (red up, green down)
controls.text: These lights show where the wheels are. A red light means the landing gear is up, and a green light means it is down and ready for landing.
controls.context: The pilot looks at the lights after moving the gear lever. Before landing, the green light must be on.

controls.name: External ordnance lights (bombs, rockets)
controls.text: These lights show which bombs or rockets are loaded on the racks under the plane. A lit lamp means that weapon is still there.
controls.context: After an attack the pilot sees at once if everything was released or if a bomb or rocket is stuck.

areas.name: Left side and engine quadrant
areas.text: The levers the pilot moves with the left hand: the engine levers, the trim wheels, the gear and flap levers.

panels.name: Left side: engine quadrant, trim, gear and flaps
panels.text: This is the left side of the cockpit. The levers there are worked with the left hand: the engine levers, the trim wheels and the levers for the wheels and the flaps.
panels.context: The pilot flies with the right hand on the stick and keeps the left hand on these levers during take-off, flight and landing.

controls.name: Throttle lever (engine power)
controls.text: This lever makes the engine stronger or weaker, like the gas pedal of a car. Here it sets the boost, the pressure with which air is pushed into the engine. Pushing it forward gives more power.
controls.context: The pilot pushes it forward for take-off and combat, and pulls it back for cruising and landing. It sits on the left side, under the left hand.

controls.name: Propeller pitch lever (RPM)
controls.text: This lever sets the propeller pitch, which means how sharply the blades bite the air. This sets how fast the engine and propeller turn. Forward is fine pitch and more RPM.
controls.context: The pilot moves it forward for take-off and combat and back for cruising. It works together with the throttle.

controls.name: Mixture lever (altitude corrector)
controls.text: This lever sets how much fuel is mixed into the engine's air. The higher the plane flies, the thinner the air, so the pilot makes the mixture leaner with altitude.
controls.context: The pilot moves it when the plane climbs. Its other name, altitude corrector, says what it is for.

controls.name: Supercharger gear lever (1st or 2nd speed)

positions.name: 1st
positions.text: The supercharger runs in its lower speed, used at low altitude.

positions.name: 2nd
positions.text: The supercharger runs in its higher speed, used at higher altitude.

controls.text: The supercharger is a pump that pushes air into the engine. This lever picks one of its two speeds, like the gears of a car. The 1st speed is for low altitude and the 2nd speed for higher altitude.
controls.context: The pilot changes to the 2nd speed when climbing high, where the air is thin, and back to the 1st speed when coming down.

controls.name: Elevator trim wheel
controls.text: This wheel adjusts the trim of the elevator, the movable part of the tail that points the nose up or down. A small turn lets the plane fly straight without the pilot pushing on the stick.
controls.context: The pilot trims after take-off and whenever the speed changes, to take the load off the right hand.

controls.name: Rudder trim wheel
controls.text: This wheel adjusts the trim of the rudder, the movable part of the tail that turns the nose left and right. A small turn keeps the plane straight without a push on the pedals.
controls.context: The engine pulls the plane a little to one side. The rudder trim takes that pull away, so the pilot's feet can rest.

controls.name: Landing gear lever

positions.name: UP
positions.text: The gear is raised into the plane.

positions.name: NEUTRAL
positions.text: The middle position. The lever rests here when the gear is not being moved.

positions.name: DOWN
positions.text: The gear is lowered, ready for landing.

controls.text: This lever raises and lowers the landing gear, the wheels and their legs. The wheels fold away in flight so that the plane flies faster. The middle position leaves the gear where it is.
controls.context: The pilot raises the gear after take-off and lowers it before landing. The red and green gear lights show what the wheels are doing.

controls.name: Flap control lever
controls.text: This lever moves the flaps, parts of the wing that fold down to give more lift at low speed. They are used for take-off and landing.
controls.context: The pilot lowers the flaps when approaching to land so the plane can fly slowly, and raises them again afterwards to fly fast.

controls.name: Cowl flap control
controls.text: This handle opens and closes the cowl flaps, doors around the engine that let the cooling air through. Open doors cool the engine better.
controls.context: The pilot opens them when the engine gets hot, for example on the ground or in a climb, and closes them for more speed.

areas.name: Right side
areas.text: The radio, the compressed-air valve, the fuel cock and the electrical switches are on the right wall.

panels.name: Right side: radio, air, fuel and electrics
panels.text: This is the right side of the cockpit. It holds the radio controls, the valve and dials for the compressed air, the fuel cock and the electrical switches.
panels.context: The pilot sets these things before and after the flight. In flight the right hand stays on the stick.

controls.name: RSI-4 radio controls
controls.text: These are the knobs of the radio set RSI-4. They tune the receiver to a radio frequency and set its volume.
controls.context: The pilot sets the radio before the flight. The transmit button is on the throttle.

controls.name: Compressed-air valve and gauges
controls.text: This is a valve and dials for the compressed air stored in bottles. The air works the wheel brakes and the flaps, and it charges the guns.
controls.context: The pilot looks at the dials to see if there is enough air. When the bottles are empty, brakes and flaps no longer work.

controls.name: Fuel cock (fuel tank selector)
controls.text: This handle is the tap for the fuel. It chooses which tank feeds the engine and can shut the fuel off.
controls.context: The pilot switches tanks to use the fuel evenly. In an emergency, such as a fire, the fuel can be shut off.

controls.name: Electrical switch panel
controls.text: This small panel holds the electrical switches of the plane. The catalog lists the generator, the lights and the gun heating among them.
controls.context: The pilot switches on the generator after the engine start, and the lights at night. The gun heating keeps the guns working in cold air.

controls.name: Primer pump (starting aid)
controls.text: This hand pump squirts a little fuel into the engine's cylinders, which makes a cold engine easier to start. The pilot moves the handle back and forth.
controls.context: The pilot uses it before the engine start, mostly on a cold day.

areas.name: Stick and throttle
areas.text: The controls that the game lets you bind to a joystick and a throttle: the stick with its grip, and the engine levers at the left hand.

panels.name: Control stick and grip
panels.text: The control stick is the main steering control of the plane. The buttons and levers on its grip fire the weapons, drop the bombs and work the wheel brakes.
panels.context: The pilot holds the stick with the right hand. In JoyPro these controls are the ones bound to a joystick grip.

controls.name: Electric firing button (cannons)
controls.text: This is the firing button of the cannons, under the index finger. Pressing it fires the ShVAK cannons of the La-5. The button sits under the guard, which has to be flipped back first.
controls.context: The pilot fires when the target is in the sight. A cannon shell is much heavier than a machine-gun bullet.

controls.name: Safety guard (trigger guard)
controls.text: This is a guard over the firing button on the stick. Flipping it back arms the button. After that the button works as the trigger.
controls.context: The guard keeps the pilot from firing by accident. Flip it back before the attack.

controls.name: Bomb-release button
controls.text: A button on top of the grip, pressed with the thumb. It releases the bombs of the La-5.
controls.context: The La-5 carries bombs under the wings in addition to its cannons. The pilot presses it over the target.

controls.name: Brake lever
controls.text: A lever on the stick grip that the pilot squeezes with the fingers to brake the wheels. The harder it is squeezed, the stronger the braking. The rudder pedals decide which wheel is braked more, so the plane can steer on the ground.
controls.context: The pilot brakes on the ground, when landing or taxiing. In the game it is an axis, so it can be bound to a throttle slider or a toe-brake.

controls.name: Control stick
controls.text: This is the control stick, the main steering control. Pushing it forward and pulling it back pitches the nose down and up. Moving it left and right rolls the plane onto its side, which starts a turn.
controls.context: On a joystick this is the main stick axis. The pilot uses it all the time, from take-off to landing.

panels.name: Engine levers and throttle
panels.text: These are the levers at the pilot's left hand: the throttle and the other engine levers, with the trim wheels and the buttons the game binds to a throttle device.
panels.context: The pilot keeps the left hand there during the whole flight. In JoyPro these controls are the ones bound to a throttle device.

controls.name: Radio-transmit button
controls.text: A button on the upper part of the throttle that the thumb presses. While it is pressed the pilot transmits by radio.
controls.context: It is the push-to-talk button. Pilots use the radio to talk to the formation and the ground.

controls.name: Mixture cutoff lever
controls.text: A lever on the engine quadrant. Pressing it stops the fuel injection pump of the engine, which the catalog names NB-3U. Without the injected fuel the engine stops.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to stop the engine on the ground. It is not a lever to touch in flight.

controls.name: Throttle lever
controls.text: This is the throttle lever on the engine quadrant at the left side. It sets the power of the ASh-82 engine, in the game as the boost pressure. Forward gives more power.
controls.context: On a joystick set this is the main throttle axis.

controls.name: Boost (forsazh)
controls.text: This is the boost mode, called forsazh in Russian. It gives the engine more power than the normal maximum. The engine is not made to run like this for long.
controls.context: The pilot uses it in an emergency or when a short burst of power wins a fight. Afterwards the throttle goes back to the normal range.

controls.name: Propeller pitch control lever
controls.text: This lever sits on the engine quadrant. It sets the propeller pitch, which decides how fast the engine and propeller turn. Forward gives a finer pitch and more RPM.
controls.context: On a throttle device it is an axis of its own, for example a slider or a second lever.

controls.name: Mixture control lever
controls.text: This lever sits on the engine quadrant. It sets how much fuel goes into the engine's air. The game can set the mixture by itself when the lever is at its middle or maximum position.
controls.context: The pilot makes the mixture leaner as the plane climbs. On a throttle device it is an axis of its own.

controls.name: Supercharger gear lever
controls.text: This lever on the left side switches the supercharger, the pump that pushes air into the engine, between its two speeds. Pulled back it is the 1st speed, pushed forward it is the 2nd.
controls.context: The pilot changes to the 2nd speed at higher altitude, where the air is thin. In the game it is bound to a button or to two buttons.

controls.name: Elevator trim wheel
controls.text: This is the elevator trim wheel on the left side. Moving it up trims the nose down, and moving it down trims the nose up. Trim lets the plane fly straight without holding the stick.
controls.context: On a joystick set it is usually a trim hat or two buttons.

controls.name: Rudder trim wheel
controls.text: This is the rudder trim wheel next to the elevator trim. Moving it left or right trims the nose in that direction, so the pilot's feet can rest.
controls.context: On a joystick set it is usually two buttons.
